newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Western Australia industrial turmoil continues.
newsitem.headline: Western Australia industrial turmoil continues.

text.p: Power restrictions continued to affect industry and commerce in the south west corner of Western Australia on Thursday as union protests against proposed changes to the state's industrial relations laws continued.
Western Power said the Australian Industrial Relations Tribunal had issued a return to work order but the restrictions would remain in force until the men returned to work.
"We don't yet know what the workers will do," a Western Power spokesman said.
"But if they don't go back to work we will continue with the restrictions and do what we can to avert power cuts."

Western Power was operating at 65 percent generating capacity because of the protest strike by 24 coal handlers at Muja power station in Collie and 50 workers at the smaller Kwinana power station in Perth.

The anti-legislation protest, which was launched on Tuesday with a rally involving an estimated 15,000 people, also involved hundreds of construction workers who walked off building sites in Perth on Thursday after four of their members manning a Workers' Embassy caravan outside State Parliament as part of the anti-legislation protest, were arrested by police on Wednesday night.
Meanwhile the state Chamber of Commerce and Industry (CCI) warned stand-downs were imminent if regular power supplies were not resumed within the next few days.

At the same time the state Trades and Labor Council, which is leading the protest against the legislation, said industrial action will continue until the Labor Relations Legislation Amendment Bill is withdrawn.
"Clearly the government intends to pass their law but the campaign will run," TLC assistent secretary, Stephanie Mayman, said.
"And if the law comes into effect we will make it unworkable."
According to the CCI, Wednesday was a lost day of production for a large number of enterprises, except for tasks such as maintenance and cleaning.
"If the restrictions continue, however, stand-downs are imminent," a CCI spokesman said.
"I heard of a few cases yesterday but the businesses concerned don't want to draw attention to themselves."
The Chamber of Minerals and Energy said most mining operations in the South West of the state and the Goldfields rely on Western Power.
"Some of the more isolated operations would use diesel and those using the Goldfield's gas pipeline would not be affected," the Chamber's Executive Officer (Public Affairs) Tony Johnson said.

"There was also a long lead time to the industrial action. In situations like this miners tend to keep their mining operations going but general processing - the production side of the operation - grinds to a halt."
An Alcoa of Australia Ltd spokesman told Reuters none of its refineries or mines were affected by the power restrictions because the company has its own power stations.
However, Westralian Sands Ltd said its mineral sands operations were completely shut down except for its synthetic rutile plant which was only using enough power to keep the kiln turning around.

"There have been no stand-downs," Westralian Sands spokesman Russell Harvie said. "All our workers have been doing regular maintenance and cleanup today and will be tomorrow as well. But if the restrictions continue next week we would have to look at
that (stand-downs)."
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
